title: Six killed in Krakow 'far-right' shooting, as three more bodies found in attacker's home
description: A gunman believed to have been inspired by far-right ideology has killed six people and injured more than a dozen others in an attack in the busy cent
body: A gunman believed to have been inspired by far-right ideology has killed six people and injured more than a dozen others in an attack in the busy centre of Poland's second largest city. Police said the attacker drove on to Main Market Square in Krakow, a popular tourist attraction, on Saturday afternoon and fired randomly at people. Four women and two men were killed. Three were Polish, one was British and two have not been identified.Among the 16 injured are five foreign nationals from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia and Britain. Another three bodies were found when counter-terrorism police searched the suspect's home around 125 miles (200km) away, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.A massive armed police presence was deployed across Krakow on Saturday evening, as security measures were ramped up in the capital Warsaw and elsewhere. A period of mourning has been declared in Krakow until 11 November. Two police officers are also among those injured, one critically.The suspect, who was equipped with military-style weapons and attire, is a 25-year-old Polish man - described by a minister as "ultra-nationalist".He has been arrested and remains in hospital after having surgery.Tusk said there were "strong indications" the two women and one man found dead at the suspect's home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski were his immediate family members.He said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism... that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "I'm shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków today.""My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in the historic centre of Krakow, an ornate square which has long been a draw for tourists. Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.The glass front of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes. Images from the scene show overturned tables and scattered belongings left behind as people ran for their lives.Armed police officers pursued the attacker's car until it crashed, at which point they engaged him in a firefight. Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify captured the moment a police officer confronted the suspect as he lay on the ground.The officer, who is visibly injured, can then be seen falling to the ground. EU foreign policy chief Kaja ⁠Kallas called the attack a "tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland."British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on social media the UK government "deeply mourns" those who died in the "appalling attack"."All of my deepest condolences go to the families of the victims," he added. The Foreign Office updated its advice, external after the attack and said people in the area should follow the guidance of local authorities.Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded.Cezary, a 24-year-old Polish university student in Krakow, said he had not realised the loud bangs he heard were gunshots until he saw four bodies lying on the street."We were still hearing gunshots, a lot of people were screaming," he said, adding that he had seen someone trying to resuscitate a person covered in blood on the ground.Caitlin Shasby, from Newcastle in the UK, said she had heard shooting from her hotel room and had been told to take shelter inside as police "barricaded" the street outside. Another witness told Polish news website Inertia: "I saw shots being fired from the driver's side window and smoke was coming out. "I ran to the police station in the main market square - when I burst inside, it was full of people hiding on the floor."

schema.headline: Six killed in Krakow 'far-right' shooting, as three more bodies found in attacker's home

title: 'Please take the job!' - Trump asks UFC boss Dana White to be White House press secretary
description: US President Donald Trump has asked Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be White House press secretary, in a social media post."Da
body: US President Donald Trump has asked Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be White House press secretary, in a social media post."Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Dana, please take the job!"It was unclear whether the president's public job offer was genuine, although White said later on Saturday: "I'm going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday".The vacancy for White House press secretary has been open since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia quit less than five days into the job.Trump's post on Saturday afternoon comes after his fellow Republicans were routed in the US midterm elections, losing their congressional majorities.The president called White "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and asked that he bring a number of high-profile UFC fighters with him on the job "even though some are not from our Country"."We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote, alongside photos of the six fighters. Following Trump's post, White posted an Instagram photo of himself behind the lectern in the White House press briefing room. "On to the next chapter," White wrote, though it was unclear if the post was tongue-in-cheek. "Hell yeah! Do it, @DanaWhite!" White House communications director Steven Cheung posted on X, as he shared the president's message.White was ringside for a fight in London on Saturday night between British former world champion Chris Billam-Smith and Jamaican-born Briton Cheavon Clarke at the Copper Box Arena.Asked about the Trump offer at a news conference afterwards, the UFC chief executive said he was flying to Washington for a meeting with Trump on Monday. "I got a lot of jobs already," he told reporters."I'm sure we'll have something to talk about after that," he added, without being drawn on whether he was interested in taking on one of the most gruelling jobs in the political arena.CNN cited a source familiar as saying that White had declined the idea.As he noted in the news conference, he already has a number of time-consuming commitments.As well as leading UFC and Power Slap, a regulated slap-fighting promotion league, he has just launched Zuffa Boxing, a professional promotion company.And last year he was unveiled as one of three new board members of Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.Famously combative, White has at times clashed with journalists covering the sport during news conferences.He released a clip in 2020 lambasting reporters who had questioned the UFC's decision to hold fights during the pandemic.In 2009, he released an expletive-laden video tirade using an anti-gay slur while rebutting a journalist's story about changes to credential rules backstage at UFC events.White is a longtime ally - and friend - of Trump.When White and his business partners bought the then-struggling UFC organisation for $2m in 2001, the sport's future seemed uncertain.Just five years earlier, Republican Senator John McCain had famously labelled mixed martial arts "human cockfighting", sparking bans in 36 US states."None of the venues wanted [the UFC]," White said in 2025. "They didn't believe in it. They didn't like it, and they were worried about the type of crowd that would show up for this type of event."With mainstream arenas shutting them out, White credits Trump with saving the organisation by hosting two UFC events at the Trump Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City, New Jersey, in 2001.White became a speaker for Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.He also appeared on stage for Trump's victory speech in the 2024 presidential election.This summer, the UFC staged a cage match on the White House lawn.

schema.headline: 'Please take the job!' - Trump asks UFC boss Dana White to be White House press secretary

title: Israel president asks opposition leader Eisenkot to form government
description: Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with
body: Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election.Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension."Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X.No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions.Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.That positions them as potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.Herzog said that, after consulting all parties during the week, he would give Eisenkot the first chance to form a government.A statement from the president's office said he had informed both Eisenkot and Netanyahu of the decision.Following consultations with delegations from the incoming Knesset members, Eisenkot received 67 recommendations for the premiership and Netanyahu 46, the statement said.The president has broad discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition and does not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.The election results had implied three possible options for the formation of a government: a national unity administration involving both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but there has been speculation that an agreement could be reached.He could also attempt to reach a deal with ultra-Orthodox parties, but that too would be difficult.There is precedent for a unity government. In 2020, following three deadlocked elections, Netanyahu and his centrist rival Benny Gantz agreed a power-sharing deal in which the leadership rotated between the two.During his consultations with the parties, Herzog had said that to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable government, he expected "factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled".In the period 2019 to 2022, one of the most politically fractured in Israeli politics, there were five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.

schema.headline: Israel president asks opposition leader Eisenkot to form government

title: The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special teased in new photos
description: New images have been revealed ahead of the Christmas special of BBC series The Other Bennet Sister.Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the
body: New images have been revealed ahead of the Christmas special of BBC series The Other Bennet Sister.Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the first series was filmed largely in Wales and attracted 6.5 million UK viewers in its first 28 days.The series finale saw Mary Bennet, played by Ella Bruccoleri, agree to marry Tom Hayward, played by Donal Finn.Filming wrapped on the three-part Christmas special at the end of August.Little has been shared about the plot of the upcoming episodes, but the BBC teased: "With marriage comes a new identity and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs Hayward?" as fans eagerly await its return.The first series of The Other Bennet Sister focused on Mary, the oft-overlooked middle sister in Pride and Prejudice, as she navigates the societal pressures of Regency England where marriage is both an aspiration and a necessity.It was mostly filmed in south Wales at locations including Merthyr Mawr in Bridgend county, the Gower peninsula, and Brecon, in Powys.The Christmas special has been produced by Cardiff-based Bad Wolf, and filming took place over the summer, also primarily in Wales.Gavin & Stacey's Ruth Jones returns to the hit show as Mrs Bennet, who she previously described as "often quite cruel" to her daughter.

schema.headline: The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special teased in new photos

title: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
description: Figure caption, Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last monthByBethany Bellin BavariaPerched on a ridge high up in the
body: Figure caption, Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last monthByBethany Bellin BavariaPerched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.Image source, Galerie Bilderwelt/Getty ImagesImage caption, Adolf Hitler used the mountain retreat to welcome guestsBefore it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.Image source, Universal Images Group via Getty ImagesImage caption, Before it was burned down, the Kehlsteinhaus or Eagle's Nest had long been a tourist destination in BavariaAround 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history."It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler committed suicide: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police say the old Nazi retreat was largely destroyed by last month's fireBut Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus."We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed."We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".Image source, ERIC SCHWAB/AFPImage caption, After Hitler's downfall, US soldiers captured the mountain-top retreat and are seen relaxing here on 4 May 1945Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question"."I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era. With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

schema.headline: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat

title: Buatsi vs Hutchinson 2: Scotland's Willy Hutchinson wins WBC light-heavyweight title
description: Willy Hutchinson was crowned the WBC light-heavyweight champion after he produced the performance of his career to beat Joshua Buatsi in Manchester.Hu
body: Willy Hutchinson was crowned the WBC light-heavyweight champion after he produced the performance of his career to beat Joshua Buatsi in Manchester.Hutchinson, 28, edged the tense rematch with the judges scoring it 117-112, 115-113, 115-113 to avenge his defeat by Buatsi in 2024.Saturday's contest was initially for the interim title but was upgraded when American David Benavidez gave up the WBC gold to move up to cruiserweight.It was a childhood dream come true for Scotland's Hutchinson, who said before the fight he wrote about his dreams of becoming a WBC champion at the age of 13.An emotional Hutchinson said after his win was confirmed: "I want to tell the story one more time. I was 13-years-old. My dad was working in Sweden. I signed it in a book, I said I will become a world champion. Let's go!"Can I say thank you to my coach because I'll you one thing, without him I don't think I'll be here today let alone boxing. This man dug me out of a hole that I never thought that I would get out of, so this is all a bonus baby."Ticket sales were modest for a world title fight as it was clear that it did not capture the attention of the British public. But those inside made the atmosphere as raucous as possible, with the Manchester crowd favouring Hutchinson.And they were delighted when the result was read out and Hutchinson became the eighth British light-heavyweight champion - the first since Nathan Cleverly in 2017.Hutchinson improved his record to 21 victories with two defeats, while it is the second time Londoner Buatsi has lost in 22 professional fights.Fight week was dominated by predictions that Buatsi, five years Hutchinson's senior, is over the hill.And the Londoner did nothing to prove otherwise as Hutchinson often toyed with his opponent in the centre of the ring.The first fight in 2024 had Buatsi walking to the ring as a comfortable favourite, and he backed that up with crushing body shots to send Hutchinson tumbling twice.But this time around, Hutchinson was a different fighter. In his own words, he had "matured" after picking up two wins since last facing Buatsi.Hutchinson clearly had the crowd on his side as he made the walk to cheers, while Buatsi was met by a chorus of boos as he paraded around the ring before the bell.For Buatsi, the strategy was very much the same as the first encounter - whip shots into the body - but Hutchinson now had answers.The AO Arena is famous for its boxing nights with the city's favourite boxing son, Ricky Hatton, becoming world champion here for the first time in June 2005 in a thriller against Kostya Tszyu.This did not reach those heights, as the upper tier was closed off because of a lack of ticket sales - and fans of Manchester's Jack Rafferty departed after he won the co-main event.This did not deter Hutchinson from advancing in the latter rounds and landing rapid triple jabs, while also switching stances.As Manchester royalty Bez, of the Happy Mondays, watched on from ringside, Hutchinson's corner told him "three rounds and you're a world champion" after the ninth.And they were right. Despite Buatsi's advances late on, Hutchinson held out to become world champion for the first time.

schema.headline: Buatsi vs Hutchinson 2: Scotland's Willy Hutchinson wins WBC light-heavyweight title

title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline HalpertRepublicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that po
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline HalpertRepublicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy."There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away. It's too early to tell which faction will win out. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency."There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist. "But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."Image source, Getty ImagesShould Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decadesDemocrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination."Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nominationOther rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race."It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said."But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."Figure caption, 'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shiftFollow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?

title: Duo-euthanasia: When your parents choose to die
description: My parents chose to die together and I was left to grieve alone Image source, BasImage caption, Bas pictured with his parents Els and Jan in 1994ByLin
body: My parents chose to die together and I was left to grieve alone Image source, BasImage caption, Bas pictured with his parents Els and Jan in 1994ByLinda PresslySome people might find this article upsetting.Early one morning in June 2024, Bas pulled up next to his parents' campervan, parked on a sunny marina in the north of the Netherlands.His father and mother, Jan and Els, had spent most of their married life on water. Now in their 70s, they could no longer manage a houseboat. Their campervan, positioned close to the yachts and dinghies, was the next best thing.Jan and Els got into their son's car. Bas started the engine. This would be the final time he drove his parents anywhere. For Jan and Els, this journey - to the local hospice - would be their last.At 10:30 that morning they would be administered lethal medication by doctors and die together in what is known in the Netherlands as duo-euthanasia. It's legal and it's rare, but every year more Dutch people choose to end their lives this way.Image source, BasImage caption, Els and Jan had spent most of their married life on water Three days before their fatal appointment at the hospice, Jan and Els gave an interview to the BBC in their campervan. Jan was living with continual pain, the legacy of years hauling cargo on the Netherlands' inland waterways. Els had been diagnosed with dementia. Their story was picked up and commented on around the world. Now, more than two years on, the couple's only child describes trying to persuade his mother and father to delay their deaths while supporting their decision to stop living. He reveals the emotional burden his parents' decision placed on him and the profound loneliness that followed.The journeyBas had planned a scenic route to the hospice, taking in Friesland's meadows and canals."I still remember the whole trip," he says. His mum was in the back seat and his dad sat beside him. At first, they talked. Els seemed resolute about their decision to opt for euthanasia."My mum was convinced, certain about doing it," Bas says. "But my dad was a little bit emotional."Jan asked his son if they were doing the right thing. Bas was thrown - he thought it would be his mum who might have doubts."My mum had always really enjoyed life," he says. "I remember she told me, 'I'd love to be 80 or maybe even 90 years old.'"But his father had been talking about euthanasia for more than a decade because of all the years of pain.In the car, Bas reassured his father. Once Jan calmed down, they drove without speaking, listened to music and watched the scenery go by.Loving, living and dying together in the Netherlands8 NovemberImage source, BasImage caption, Els and Jan, pictured here in 1977, were keen racing sailorsIn the months before the family made this journey, Bas had tried to persuade his parents to delay their deaths."I tried to convince them to stay a bit longer - why not wait until winter, or next year?"Bas was conflicted. Although he thought his parents' decision to ask for euthanasia was the right one, he didn't want them to go."My dad, he was in this situation for 10 to 15 years, so he could probably have stretched it for another few years. But I think waiting for another year, then my mum would get into trouble…"If Els delayed applying for euthanasia, she risked her Alzheimer's worsening, which might mean she would not be deemed capable of making the decision to end her own life.At the hospiceBas found a parking space."My dad said goodbye to my car - he liked my car, and he said, 'Good job', and 'thank you'."And then we walked inside," Bas says. "Imagine doing that - being in their shoes, taking that trip and that walk. It's so unreal."For the next two hours, the couple's family and friends came and went. They reminisced, and listened to music. At one point, it crossed Bas' mind to call a halt to the proceedings."I had a feeling - 'OK, let's leave… Let's step into the car and drive away,'" he says. "But I didn't want to bring anything up that would make them feel uncertain - I had supported the whole [euthanasia] process."Better to keep everybody calm, and take the moment to say goodbye."Just before 10:30am, doctors arrived to inject Jan and Els with the lethal medication that would kill them. The couple lay on hospital beds side by side. And in those final moments, before they lost consciousness, Bas witnessed his parents' closeness."I've seen them maybe three or four times in all my life walking hand in hand," he says. "But now they were laying there, hand in hand. And that gave me a really good feeling - they're really doing this together."Bas describes that first half hour after his parents stopped breathing as "a factual thing" - they weren't alive anymore."Then you realise what the situation is - that's an unimaginable feeling."Where to get help- The Samaritans, external- Befrienders Worldwide, external- NHS Help for suicidal thoughts, external- BBC Action LineImage source, BasImage caption, Jan coached hockey - and often took his son along with himIn the hospice, sorrow hit Bas. He began to experience a profound loneliness."Grieving is a very, very deep thing to go through," he says, "and I don't have brothers and sisters - I really felt alone."If we've been brought up by two parents, when the first dies, we can share our memories and sadness with the other as part of the process of bereavement. But Jan and Els were both gone."It was like my legs were cut off," remembers Bas.His grief was physical too - he felt sick for four or five weeks. His body hurt."I would not really recommend this to others, and that's maybe a hard conclusion," he says. "It was maybe for them [my parents] the best option, but having lost them both at the same moment was very, very impactful."Image source, BasImage caption, Els and Jan took Bas to watch sailing competitions when he was a childDid Jan and Els go too soon?Among people planning to apply for euthanasia in the Netherlands, especially those with dementia like Els, choosing the right moment to end your life may be complicated.9,958 people in the Netherlands chose death by euthanasia in 2024427 of those who chose death by euthanasia in 2024 had dementia - six had advanced dementia108 people chose death by duo-euthanasia (54 pairs) that yearSource: Regional Euthanasia Review Committees (RTE)As well as demonstrating they are suffering unbearably, they must be assessed by doctors as still having the capacity to decide for themselves they want to die. This can cause immense distress in dementia patients thinking about euthanasia, explains Dr Rozemarijn van Bruchem, a geriatrician and ethicist at the Erasmus Medical Centre in Rotterdam."They think… I have that power right now, but now is too soon. But maybe next month is too late. So how do I decide at what point I need to start this process to see if I meet the criteria, to see if I can get euthanasia? And if I wait too long, might I have missed the window?"Dr van Bruchem says it's because euthanasia is legal in the Netherlands that her patients experience this anxiety. And they know permission for an assisted death in cases of advanced dementia is rare. In countries where euthanasia is prohibited, like the UK, people with dementia may face many challenges, but they rarely have to weigh these life-or-death options - as Els did.In 2024, she told the BBC that she and her husband couldn't wait because there was a chance her Alzheimer's would progress. And Jan was committed to dying with Els. He told the BBC that perhaps he was going too soon, but he had lived his life – his life was completed.Was everything said?Image source, BasImage caption, Bas inherited his parents' love of boats and waterJan and Els were very aware of the burden their end-of-life decisions placed on their son. Bas attended all the meetings his parents had with their separate doctors during the euthanasia process. There were open family discussions. Often, we have regrets when a loved-one dies – especially about what may have been left unspoken. This didn't happen to Bas. Two days before Jan and Els' appointment at the hospice on Monday 3 June he wrote them a letter."It was about eight pages," Bas says. "I went to the campervan late in the evening on Saturday night, two days before the event. I read the whole letter to them. It was about our lives, thanking them for what they'd done."Jan and Els were deeply moved. And just as they rarely displayed affection to each other in public, they hadn't usually been demonstrative with their son either."You feel that they love you, but it's shown by doing stuff, not really saying it, or giving you a hug," says Bas. "My mum did [hug] more when she got dementia, but my dad never did – I never got a hug."That changed in the campervan on that last Saturday night. Jan hugged Bas."He did it after that letter.  It was maybe one of the best moments."Everything was said."

schema.headline: Duo-euthanasia: When your parents choose to die

title: How property, football and politics link Manchester and Abu Dhabi
description: Property, football and politics: The links between Manchester and Abu Dhabi explainedImage source, PA MediaImage caption, The Abu Dhabi United Group t
body: Property, football and politics: The links between Manchester and Abu Dhabi explainedImage source, PA MediaImage caption, The Abu Dhabi United Group took over Manchester City in 2008ByMat TrewernBBC North WestWhen Manchester City was found guilty in September of breaching Premier League financial rules, the damning and unprecedented verdict left the football world reeling.An independent commission said the club had "systematically" broken rules between 2009 and 2018 by inflating sponsorship revenue to disguise secret funding of more than £830m into its football operations.Speculation is now rife about the level of punishment City will face, although the club denies any wrongdoing and has appealed against the ruling.While we await the outcome, the historical relationship between City's Abu Dhabi-based owners and Manchester's political elite - including the now Prime Minister Andy Burnham - has been in the spotlight.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan (centre) bought Man City in a £200m dealThere has been a focus on land deals, multimillion-pound regeneration schemes, and more recently, investigations into loans handed out to property companies owned ultimately by City's owner, the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).Beyond the on-field success at the Eithad Stadium, what exactly is the Abu Dhabi story in Manchester?The story began in 2008 when Manchester City was bought by ADUG in a £200m deal. The Citizens were now owned by Sheikh Mansour, the United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister and a member of its ruling family.Overnight, City had become one of the richest clubs in the world.In the years that followed, City's new owners spent billions of pounds turning the club into one of European football's powerhouses.But away from the pitch, the Abu Dhabi investors were showing a wider interest in their new adopted city of Manchester.Image source, Action Images/ReutersImage caption, Manchester City's owners have invested in club, commercial and community developments in East ManchesterIn 2014, six years after taking over Manchester City, ADUG entered into a partnership with Labour-led Manchester City Council.The club and the council already had a close relationship, with Manchester City having signed a 250-year lease for the former City of Manchester Stadium that had been built for the 2002 Commonwealth Games.The new joint venture was called Manchester Life and, over a decade, it had a plan to build more than 6,000 new homes through investment of up to £1bn.To date, about 1,500 homes across nine sites have been delivered, with more currently under construction.ADUG has also financially supported local community facilities, including the East Manchester Leisure Centre, which opened in 2014.The area around the stadium was also extensively redeveloped into what is now known as the Etihad Campus, which is also home to the Sky Blues' women's and youth teams.Most recently, Co-op Live - the largest indoor arena in the UK - opened next to Etihad Stadium and became another high-profile development in east Manchester in which ADUG held a significant stake.Bev Craig, the recently elected Mayor of Greater Manchester, said ADUG had shown a "unique passion" and commitment to Manchester.Speaking to the BBC in 2024 while in her previous job as leader of Manchester City Council, Craig described City's owners as having been the "catalyst" for "remarkable" regeneration.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig insists the city has benefited from its partnership with Abu DhabiHowever, there have been repeated claims that the city council sold public land to ADUG too cheaply.In 2022, a report by the University of Sheffield raised questions about the wider public value of the schemes and a lack of transparency surrounding their finances.These claims are strongly rejected by Manchester's political leaders, including Sir Richard Leese, who led the city council when the ADUG deal was struck in 2014."The point is, the investment from Abu Dhabi is what created the value," Sir Richard told the BBC recently.He stressed, like Craig and the city council itself, that there was no other significant interest in developing the land during a time of recession following the 2008 financial crash."It was a time when development in Manchester had stopped," said Sir Richard."That deal allowed development to be kick-started - particularly in the Ancoats area."Image caption, The Abu Dhabi United Group has partnered with Manchester City Council to regenerate Ancoats and New IslingtonCertainly the areas around Ancoats and New Islington, which had suffered from the industrial decline of the latter part of the 20th Century, have been transformed.Critics, though, are quick to point out the lack of any affordable housing within the Abu Dhabi-owned flats and apartments.The city council, however, says the regeneration has led to more recent developments in the area, and that these do include social and affordable homes.The agreement made between Manchester City Council and ADUG is known as an "overage" deal.It means the seller of the land - in this case the local authority - receives extra financial payments in the future if the land increases in value after it is sold.These payments are a share of the so-called "super profits".While these sorts of deals can be complex, they have become increasingly common between local authorities and developers.Manchester City Council said allegations that its deal with ADUG had either not been good for the local authority or its taxpayers had been "debunked repeatedly".It said the council had made just under £3m in "super-profits" from Abu Dhabi-owned developments so far, and expected another payment soon.Prof Adam Leaver, co-author of the University of Sheffield report, has argued that commercial secrecy around the arrangements mean it is hard to know if the council has got the best possible deal.He said it was "not possible" to know how much profit ADUG had made from the developments, compared to that of the city council.Leaver also challenged the assertion that there had been little other interest in redeveloping Manchester around the time the Manchester Life partnership was formed.He pointed out that a number of large projects had already been in the pipeline.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matchesScrutiny of the land development deal and the wider relationship between Manchester City's owners and the city council intensified after Burnham's comments about the club's breaches of Premier League financial rules.The prime minister and former Greater Manchester mayor said he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners sold up and praised them for being a "huge partner in the building of modern Manchester".There was an immediate backlash, with some suggesting Burnham was siding with the club. Downing Street then stated Manchester City was not "above the rules", and stressed the PM had made it clear that the outcome of the "ongoing independent process" must be respected.Nevertheless, questions remained. It then emerged that Burnham, while in his role as the city region's mayor, had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City's chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018. He also met Al Mubarek at a Global Investment Summit in 2021.Burnham's political opponents have demanded full transparency over his dealings with Manchester City's owners. He recently told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, An investigation will be held into public loans made to property firms, including some belonging to Manchester City's Abu Dhabi-based ownersThere will also be a Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) scrutiny committee investigation into GMCA loans made to property companies - including three controlled by Manchester City's owner - while Burnham was mayor.More than £1bn was lent to about 50 developers by the Greater Manchester Housing Investment Loan Fund. Burnham chaired two meetings which approved about £55m in loans to property firms ultimately owned by Man City's owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan.The decisions were made in public by all members of the GMCA, not the mayor alone. There is no suggestion of any wrongdoing, but critics have questioned why seemingly wealthy and successful companies needed to borrow public money through the scheme.Craig said the intense coverage of Manchester's relationship with Abu Dhabi had made "cheap shots" at Burnham and been used to "bash" the city.She said that were Manchester City to lose its appeal, then it "should face sanctions".But she was keen to stress that "what was a football story should have stayed a football story".Not everyone agrees, however, and while the football world holds its breath to find out City's fate, we can also expect the spotlight to remain on the wider relationship between the city of Manchester and the club's owners.

schema.headline: How property, football and politics link Manchester and Abu Dhabi

title: Scotland's familiar frailties brutally exposed in All Blacks schooling
description: Figure caption, Highlights: Scotland 21-43 New ZealandByBBC Scotland's chief sports writerFair play to the All Blacks. At least this time they didn't
body: Figure caption, Highlights: Scotland 21-43 New ZealandByBBC Scotland's chief sports writerFair play to the All Blacks. At least this time they didn't wait until the closing minutes to put Scotland away, they took them out of their misery way earlier than that. A small mercy, in a sense.No dramas, no late moments of All Black genius required, no clutch try to swing it in the end and break Scottish hearts. Those late sucker-punches? They're the worst.It's easier this way. You know where you are with shellackings. It's the near misses that are harder to take.If you're going to lose to the All Blacks, maybe it's better to be routed than robbed, better to be outclassed than walking away with a sense of grievance or a feeling a win was left behind.This was a systematic dismantling, all over in the 51st minute when Beauden Barrett, as much of a genius now at the age of 35 as he ever was, scored his second try of the day.Barrett is now on 50 Test tries and 148 caps. Murrayfield witnessed one of the all-time greats on Saturday; classy, intelligent and ruthless. Any notion Scotland could bring an end to 121 years without a win against New Zealand was trampled underfoot by Barrett and his band of brothers; blood brothers and otherwise.All Blacks get turned on by adversityThe first half was a thrill-fest, the second half was an annihilation. At the break, with Ewan Ashman having completed his hat-trick and Murrayfield rocking, the great Richie McCaw stood away to the side, just below the media gantry.Was he ashen-faced - or Ashman-faced - at the space Scotland were finding and the tries they were scoring? Was he fretful this just might be the day the record tumbles?Er, no. He took out his phone and started tapping in the manner of a guy ordering a taxi - for Scotland, of course. McCaw, and every All Black in his wake, don't worry in moments like this.They just up the ante and back themselves. They increase the intensity, the accuracy, the power. They feast on mistakes and accelerate away.The second half was 19-0 to the All Blacks. That's what outstanding rugby teams do. Away from home against a dangerous team in front of a loud crowd. They embrace adversity. They get turned on by it.Dave Rennie's favourite word, in a rugby context, is brutal, as in brutal physicality, brutal execution, brutal in putting a foot on an opponent's throat and keeping it there. All of that was visited upon Scotland. New Zealand were better and smarter. Their rugby IQ was on a different level.Scotland defence mired in quicksandImage source, SNSImage caption, Former Glasgow Warriors head coach Dave Rennie, right, enjoyed a truiumphant return to Scotland with the All BlacksGregor Townsend and his players spoke later about where it all went wrong. Didn't take enough of their chances in the first half, didn't make it hard enough for New Zealand to get field position, didn't survive at the breakdown, didn't deliver on discipline, didn't look after ball.All true, but the greater truth is that after three close Tests under Townsend since 2017, New Zealand have now pulled miles clear of Scotland.Townsend can talk about all the little things and some of the big things Scotland got wrong but these things didn't suddenly afflict his team. They didn't just drop out of the sky. They're in the DNA of this team. We have seen these failings before in defeat and even in victory.Scotland's attack can be a thing of wonder, capable of creating space and delivering sensational tries against the very best teams on the planet. They did it on Saturday against the All Blacks, they did it against South Africa in July, they did it against France and Ireland in March. These are good rugby players.The elite teams pride themselves on defence - and that's where Scotland are mired in quicksand. They conceded five tries in defeat to the Pumas last autumn. In victory, they put 50 on France but conceded 40 points and six tries.They shipped 43 points against Ireland and another six tries. They lost 42-18 to the Boks in the summer and gave up another six tries. They beat the Pumas but, again, their inability to be savage on the other side of the ball saw them conceding 38 points and five tries. It was another 40-pointer against the All Blacks - and another six tries.Townsend must repair morale as Wallabies awaitThere were lovely moments in all of those Tests, but Scotland's big mantra coming into the autumn was all about making life difficult for opponents, making sure every yard they made in possession was only won after a battle, every try they scored was only achieved after fighting for their lives through the phases.Worthy sentiments and an important mission statement, but four minutes into it on Saturday, New Zealand threw a bit of trickery at Scotland at a lineout and scored with ease.The piece of deception - two runners bolting off a lineout as decoy men - has been done by a few teams already this season. It wasn't a revelation but it was enough to fool Scotland.The irony came in the name of the scorer. Scotland wanted their defence to be Braveheart in its, well, brutality. Wallace Sititi scored that first try. The back-row was named after William Wallace. So much for freedom from concession of soft scores.The All Blacks got to 43 points with 12 minutes left. They could have had more, but they'd made their point. They're back. Not at Springbok level, clearly, but improving.Rennie, and his sidekick Mike Blair, have brought huge improvement in a relatively short time. These All Blacks are light years ahead of the version Scott Robertson brought here 12 months ago.Townsend must now piece together shattered morale and go again next Sunday. The Wallabies are up next. Scotland have won four of their past five against Australia, all under Townsend, and will be expected to make it five from six.The Wallabies will fancy a crack at them, though. They'll respect Scotland's ability with ball in hand but relish a shot at exposing the weakness in their ranks. You don't need 20-20 vision to spot the frailties in this team. The All Blacks found them with ease in that sobering second-half schooling.

schema.headline: Scotland's familiar frailties brutally exposed in All Blacks schooling

title: Royal Family join veterans and families at Festival of Remembrance
description: Figure caption, Senior royals attend annual Royal British Legion Festival of RemembranceKing Charles III led senior members of the Royal Family as the
body: Figure caption, Senior royals attend annual Royal British Legion Festival of RemembranceKing Charles III led senior members of the Royal Family as they paid tribute to British service personnel at this year's Festival of Remembrance.The Prince of Wales and Catherine, Princess of Wales, joined the King and Queen Camilla at London's Royal Albert Hall to commemorate those who lost their lives in service, on the eve of Remembrance Sunday.The audience stood and a fanfare played as the royals entered the concert hall for the annual event, which was also attended by bereaved families and serving personnel.The King will lead the nation in two minutes of silence on Sunday to remember those who died serving in the two world wars and other conflicts.He will be joined by other senior royals and political leaders at the annual National Service of Remembrance ceremony at the Cenotaph in central London, where they will lay wreaths.Some 10,000 veterans will take part in the Royal British Legion's march-past, representing more than 300 different armed forces and civilian organisations.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Catherine wore the Irish Guards regimental brooch, earrings that once belonged to the late Queen Elizabeth II and a handmade poppyImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The King became patron of the Royal British Legion in 2024The Royal British Legion's festival, which was broadcast on BBC One at 21:00, was hosted by Clive Myrie and included performances by musicians such as Alfie Boe and Mica Paris.The Chelsea Pensioners - retired British Army veterans - were also among those in attendance, while several armed forces bands took to the stage to perform, including the Band of Royal Air Force Regiment.This year's festival marks the 35th anniversary of the end of the First Gulf War and 15 years since the conclusion of British military operations in Iraq under Operation Telic, with veterans sharing their personal stories and experiences of the conflicts.Last year, Prince George joined the King, Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales at the concert for what was thought to be the first time.Image source, Getty ImagesPrime Minister Andy Burnham and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting were also present.Events will take place around the country to mark Remembrance Sunday, which is observed on the closest Sunday to Armistice Day on 11 November - when World War One ended in 1918.The prime minister said: "Remembrance Sunday gives us an opportunity, not only to mark that sacrifice and offer our gratitude, but also to reflect on its significance. To reflect on the selflessness and courage it takes to commit your life to protecting others."I want to offer my personal thanks to those who served and those who continue to serve in our Armed Forces communities to this day."

schema.headline: Royal Family join veterans and families at Festival of Remembrance

title: Sao Paulo Grand Prix: Lando Norris and George Russell hoping for more rain in race after wet qualifying
description: Qualifying conditions borderline - but Norris and Russell hoping for more rainImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, McLaren's Lando Norris (right)
body: Qualifying conditions borderline - but Norris and Russell hoping for more rainImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, McLaren's Lando Norris (right) and George Russell were the fastest two drivers in qualifying, but the Mercedes man will start seventh in Sao Paulo because of a five-place grid penaltyByF1 CorrespondentLando Norris says qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix brought "some of the wettest conditions" in which he had ever driven - and he is hoping for more rain in the race on Sunday.It was the third consecutive year in which Norris has taken pole in Brazil, and it came in a session that was stopped for nearly an hour and a half because conditions were too dangerous to continue when officials initially tried to start it.Many drivers agreed that conditions were borderline in the extreme.Mercedes driver George Russell, who qualified second to Norris and was miffed about a team miscommunication that he felt robbed him of pole, said: "Q1 was extremely challenging. The visibility was zero down the straight into Turn Four. I was wheel-spinning in fifth gear, over 200km/h (120mph), aquaplaning."When you're aquaplaning on the straight and you can't see in front of you, it's... I'm not even sure what the word is to describe it."It does seem a bit crazy. I guess that's what we have to deal with."I love driving in the rain. I love driving in the rain here, but at some point, if that was a race, there was no way we should be driving in that because the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident are very, very high."The rain - combined with grid penalties for four of the usual front-runners, including Russell - has produced an unfamiliar grid with several drivers exploiting the opportunity of the weather to produce their best results of the year.Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson - who still does not know whether he has a seat next year - and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg occupy the second row.Haas driver Oliver Bearman is sixth, and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso and Williams' Alex Albon in eighth and ninth both made it into the top 10 for the first time in 2026.Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who won this race in the wet two years ago from 17th on the grid, start 20th and 21st after replacing their engines and exceeding their allowance for the year.Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc, who qualified fourth, has a 10-place penalty, also for engine usage.Sunday's forecast is for light rain, and the unpredictability of the weather at the Interlagos track, which is famous for it, means the teams and drivers will be open-minded about what to expect.Norris had not taken pole since the Spanish Grand Prix in September, and although his McLaren has upgrades on it, which he acknowledged had improved the car, he felt he owed it to the conditions."We're lucky it's wet, because if it was dry, I wouldn't be sitting here," said Norris. "In the dry, we definitely didn't have the pace."We've looked better this weekend but we still had some small issues, and we've not been up to the pace of the Mercedes. The wet kind of gave me an opportunity and I made the most of it."I'm hoping for a wet race. There's a good likelihood it'll be wet. There's a bit of rain, I think, tomorrow at times, and it'll still be damp through the day, so we could just have an exciting race with a little bit of everything, honestly."These are conditions where you feel like you can make a little bit more of a difference at times, for sure. And I feel like I'm against good guys who also have the capabilities of going for pole, and today we managed to do it because I put two good laps together and I had a good gap, and we managed things well."It was tense when you want to push so much. You need to kind of learn about the conditions, but you also need to not make a single mistake."But actually, I felt pretty confident through the whole of qualifying. Q3 was definitely the trickiest because it was also difficult to see, because of the light, where were the dry bits, the wet bits and puddles, things like that. So, more rewarding."Russell reminds himself 'I haven't forgotten how to drive'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, George Russell dropped to fourth in the drivers' championship from second after last weekend's Mexico City Grand PrixFor Russell, there was another disappointment in a season that has been full of them.Last weekend, he had to watch team-mate Kimi Antonelli clinch the world title and become the youngest champion in history.Here, he felt pole was his had he not been told to back off on what he felt would have been his fastest lap after he came across Albon in the twisty middle sector.The team felt the imminent heavier rain would hold off long enough for him to do another lap. They were wrong, and Russell swore over the radio asking what had happened.He was reminded by team boss Toto Wolff that he was still P2, to which he responded, short-tempered, that he was not there to be second.It might have seemed a loss of perspective, given his five-place grid penalty meant he would not have been on pole even if he had been fastest.But for Russell his feelings were rooted in self-validation after a difficult year, and it was not related to the fact that it promoted Antonelli to second."Gives me the confidence and reminds me again that I haven't forgotten how to drive," he said. "That's important in circumstances like these and it would have meant a lot to me to clinch the pole with a great performance like we showed in qualifying."He added: "I felt really confident in the rain. I think my pace, along with Lando's, was by far the best out there."In the rain here, it's always a challenge. I hope it is wet tomorrow. I feel I've got a greater chance if it's wet."Alonso back at the sharp endImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso said his tyres were "ice cold" in Q3The wet conditions provided Alonso with a chance to demonstrate the waste of talent that this year's uncompetitive Aston Martin-Honda car has created.With its down-on-power and difficult engine, Alonso has been struggling all year. There have been few chinks of light.This was a rare opportunity to shine, and he took it.Up at the sharp end throughout, he dropped away - if only relatively - in the final session when he could not get temperature in his tyres. It may have been because he was first in the queue in the pit lane in his eagerness to get in a lap time before the rain worsened again."We took some risks in Q1, in Q2, where the conditions were a little bit unknown for everybody and we made it through and then our first Q3 of the year, so obviously pleased with that," Alonso said."Then in Q3 I was expecting maybe a little bit more. I was first on the queue. But the tyres were ice cold in Q3, so I had no grip."But yeah, I look at the times now, I think P6 is 1.8 seconds in front of me. So yeah, it's way too much, you know, in front to really dream about any higher positions."There is less time full throttle (in the wet), because there is no grip. So obviously they cannot exploit the extra power."But still the engine is very important in terms of drivability and the way it behaves in the corners. We still have a little bit of an issue there."But no, I think these conditions is more about the level of risk you want to take. There is a little bit of aquaplaning here and there."Alonso joins Norris and Russell in hoping for a wet race, feeling that if it's dry he will inevitably sink back to Aston Martin's natural level, especially with the long pit straight where Honda's lack of power will render him defenceless.Hamilton and Leclerc 'moving on' after talksImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc in conversation on Saturday morning in Sao PauloThe race promises much with Leclerc, Hamilton and Verstappen all aiming to make progress from the back, even if the drivers feel that overtaking at Interlagos will be harder in this year's new-style cars than before.For Ferrari, it has been a difficult weekend, that started with clear-the-air talks between Leclerc and Hamilton after their first-lap battle cost them victory in Mexico last weekend.Both took new internal combustion engines, which gave them 10-place grid penalties, and then Hamilton's brand new one broke in final practice. So Ferrari gave him another one, leaving him at the back with Verstappen.The two multiple champions will be in competition to see who can make progress faster, and perhaps Ferrari are not so unhappy that Hamilton and Leclerc are separated by six places on the grid.Both drivers said all was well after their chat on Thursday evening.Leclerc - who returned to Europe between the two races to be at the birth of his first child, a daughter named Bianca - said: "It was good to speak. This is always needed after a moment like this. It took proportions that are way too big, but it has been around also for way too long."At the same time, it was a very special week for me, so I couldn't really have those discussions before. And it was important to have those discussions, but now I consider that a closed chapter, and it will be important to look ahead."I really believe that when we speak, things are much better straight away. Of course, there is tension. Of course, we want to finish ahead of each other, and sometimes we are not going to do things right. And it's OK sometimes to disagree on the way you see things, but at the same time, discussing about those then helps a whole lot."Hamilton added: "Me and Charles sat and spoke and we squashed it, and we're moving on."We still have a huge amount of respect for each other and I'm glad we had a chat and now we move on."We've been getting along just fine as normal. Sometimes in those scenarios it takes having a conversation and there's been no demands from either side."It's both just giving our points and areas we can do better and support each other."Sao Paulo starting grid after penalties1. Lando Norris (McLaren)2. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)3. Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls)4. Nico Hulkenberg (Audi)5. Isack Hadjar (Red Bull)6. Oliver Bearman (Haas)7. George Russell (Mercedes)8. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)9. Alex Albon (Williams)10. Oscar Piastri (McLaren)11. Rafael Camara (Haas)12. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)13. Carlos Sainz (Williams)14. Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)15. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)16. Pierre Gasly (Alpine)17. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)18. Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)19. Gabriel Bortoleto (Audi)20. Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari)21. Max Verstappen (Red Bull)22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac)
