title: Veterans shouldn't sleep rough this Christmas, Burnham says
description: Burnham will ask local authorities to use part of the additional £874m already announced to tackle homelessness specifically for housing veterans."Peo
body: Burnham will ask local authorities to use part of the additional £874m already announced to tackle homelessness specifically for housing veterans."People who stepped forward prepared to put their lives on the line for the rest of us should never lack a roof over their head," Burnham said in a statement issued on Saturday. "When they need help, the country owes them more than warm words. It owes them a bed every night, a proper plan and someone in their corner from day one."The PM will ask councils to work with local organisations and charities to tackle homelessness amongst veterans.Downing Street said an additional £8.7m in funding would be allocated to eight organisations across the UK to help housing providers offer assistance to veterans with complex needs, including those with health or addiction problems.Among them are Veteran Housing Scotland, Launchpad and SSAFA, the Armed Forces Charity.The pledge, announced ahead of Remembrance Sunday, is part of Burnham's wider plan to offer everyone currently sleeping rough a bed this winter.The most recent official figures estimated that there were 4,793 people sleeping rough, external on a single night in autumn 2025 in England - a record high. The number of people recorded as sleeping rough has been on the rise since 2021.The government has committed £4.4bn in total to end rough sleeping.Burnham previously faced criticism from the Conservatives for failing to end rough sleeping while he was the mayor of Greater Manchester. He argued that Manchester's scheme attracted rough sleepers from the surrounding regions, adding that "it's only if everywhere does it at the same level that you can actually end rough sleeping".Liberal Democrats defence spokesman James MacCleary MP said the funding was an "important first step" but that "a one-off cash injection won't fix a crisis years in the making".He urged Burnham to guarantee long-term funding for councils to tackle homelessness "for good" and to put in place measures to prevent veterans "falling through the cracks in the first place".The prime minister is urging any veterans who are sleeping rough, or those supporting them, to call a UK-wide helpline on 0800 9520774 to be connected directly to housing and other specialist support.Separately on Sunday, the culture secretary set out the UK's renewed participation in the EU's Erasmus programme of educational and cultural exchanges for young people after six years.The UK will rejoin the programme in January, enabling students and other young people to study, train or get work experience in the EU.In the announcement, Nandy added: "As we remember the immense courage of those who served our country, we honour them by building the best opportunities for the next generation through closeness and collaboration with our allies."Conservative Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake responded by saying veterans had not fought for a "student exchange scheme".He argued that it was "tone deaf and frankly shameful" to announce this on Remembrance Sunday."It is not a day for a Labour minister to try to make an EU membership pitch," the Tory chairman added.

schema.headline: Veterans shouldn't sleep rough this Christmas, Burnham says

title: Ambika Mod: Ceiling is getting higher for South Asian actors
description: She has previously spoken about not having access to the same "privilege", external some of her fellow actors do when it comes to roles. Fans have que
body: She has previously spoken about not having access to the same "privilege", external some of her fellow actors do when it comes to roles. Fans have questioned why she hasn't gone on to appear in as many roles as her One Day co-star Leo Woodall, who's since appeared in major films including Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy and A24's Anthony Bourdain biopic, Tony.Addressing this remark, Mod tells Newsbeat she thinks "there's definitely an issue in this industry with systemic racism"."I think it is really hard for South Asian actors to really push through. "I feel like the glass ceiling is always getting higher and higher and higher."A report from the Creative Diversity Network, external suggested that representation of minority ethnic groups on and off-screen dropped slightly last year, after a few years of improvement.And similar research from media watchdog Ofcom , externalfound people from certain backgrounds are less well-represented across the UK broadcasting industry.It said "people from minority ethnic groups (across the industry as a whole) only account for 11% of those in senior management roles".It also found under-representation in creative, production and on-screen roles.Mod says she doesn't know if on-screen representation is changing, but says she "won't engage" with a role if she thinks its tokenistic or stereotypical."I've been very, very lucky in my career so far from very early on to play really complex, meaty roles and to have changed the narrative in many ways," she says."And I'm not looking to regress."And when it comes to considering what to take on next, she says she tries to follow advice Dame Emma Thompson once gave her: "There's no such thing as a career, there's only what you do next.""I'm always just trying to focus on what the new challenging thing is going to be, or cool people that I want to work with," she says."And also what's going to be fun, as well."Her latest role as Laila, a lawless agent of the covert Black Doves, attracted her as it subverted a lot of espionage genre tropes.The character is introduced in season two to assist Keira Knightley's agent Helen on a mission as the stakes get even higher for those working with the secretive organisation. Mod says it was "such a good time" working alongside Knightley and getting to do some extreme stunt sequences together. "Honestly, the main reason I wanted to do it was because of all the stunts," she says."Really badass but it was so much fun. "It was just so fun to take down an absolutely staggering number of men in every single episode." The thriller also has a dark humour to it, which aligns well with Mod who often brings a dry wit to her characters.Her comedic career goes back to when she was about 18, and while studying at Durham University she was part of its sketch comedy group.Despite having not done stand-up for about five years, she says she would "love" to do more comedy in the future."I do sometimes think about going back to it," she reveals."I have a lot of stories to tell."

schema.headline: Ambika Mod: Ceiling is getting higher for South Asian actors

title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, says Barnier
description: The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy B
body: The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe.The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago.But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access.He said there was not a "single market à la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt.Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member.But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members.He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms"."There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market."Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.His predecessors have struck a series of deals with the EU on different aspects of how the UK and EU interact post-Brexit.Both sides are hoping to use a meeting in Brussels in 10 days' time to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime. Of the four freedoms, the free movement of people - which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa - was a key issue during the 2016 Brexit referendum.Burnham's immediate predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, ruled out re-establishing it for the UK in Labour's 2024 election manifesto and any move to advocate it again would prove a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at a future poll.Burnham recently said in an interview that he would not re-establish free movement of people without a referendum, prompting Downing Street to clarify that he was not advocating its return at this point.He has previously said he wanted to lay out "different options" for the relationship with Europe at the Brussels summit later this month, before trying to find a consensus with the British public on a new relationship.Barnier also predicted that EU countries would reject reinstating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget while it was a member.The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he said, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table".Barnier also compared Reform leader Nigel Farage to French politician Marine Le Pen. He said: "We have our own Farage. It is Mrs Le Pen. The same populism, the same lies, the same false promises."Asked by Kuenssberg to clarify what he was referring to with his accusation of lies, Barnier said "for instance, when Mr Farage and Mr Johnson promised the UK people to get back [£350] million per week, it was not true, it was not possible. It was a lie".The Vote Leave campaign, of which Boris Johnson became a key figure, has been criticised previously for the slogan on the side of their campaign bus that said Britain sent £350m a week to the EU, adding: "Let's fund our NHS instead". Johnson said in 2017 that "once we have settled our accounts, we will take back control of roughly £350m per week. It would be a fine thing as many of us have pointed out if a lot of that money went on the NHS". Critics have said that the £350m per week was an approximate sum which represents a "gross contribution" and did not take into account the UK's £75m-a-week rebate nor the EU's investments in the UK.Johnson has since defended the claim, saying the £350m was based on the UK's gross contribution to the EU, and was in fact an underestimate as UK contributions were due to rise. ​In his memoirs published in 2024, Johnson said EU money spent in the UK was not "democratically controlled by the British people", and "even if the net figure was only £175m, that was still a hell of a lot of money".Farage, who led Leave UK and was not part of the Vote Leave campaign so not connected to the £350m claim, said: "It is the same old Barnier - arrogant, out of touch and a bully. He vindicates our decision to leave every time he opens his mouth."

schema.headline: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, says Barnier
